sourceObservations.observations: Title identifies Lecture19 Manipulator–Mechanism Design-II and printed page1; no teaching claim.
Learning outcomes list redundancy/closed chain, actuation/transmission, stiffness/compliance, sensing and mobile manipulation; no added equations.

Redundancy for general six-coordinate pose, distal fast precise micromanipulation and closed-loop definition. Seven-DOF infinity-of-solutions and avoidance claims need reachable regular pose and feasible constraints; six-DOF finite solutions also generic rather than universal at degeneracy.

Moving top platform and base connected through three visible telescoping legs, closed contour dashed red; schematic must not be counted as full Stewart six legs. Motoman L-3 joints2/3 drive-loop source attribution. Typical stiffness benefit versus joint-range/workspace cost, not universal topology theorem.

Six telescoping legs connect the base and moving platform in the drawing. Each base connection is universal (2 DOF), each top connection is spherical (3 DOF), and each leg has a prismatic actuator (1 DOF). The source calls this a fully parallel, 6-DOF mechanism. Inverse kinematics reduces to attachment distances for a specified pose; forward kinematics is more complex, not universally unsolvable. Stiffness and load capacity trade against range of motion.

The displayed mobility equation is F = 6(l - n - 1) + sum(f_i). The legend defines l as links including ground, n as joints, and f_i as each joint mobility. Six universal, six spherical and six prismatic joints give 18 joints and a joint-mobility sum of 36. Counting alone presumes independent constraints and does not certify singularity-free motion.

The worked count uses 12 actuator members plus the base and moving platform, giving 14 links. Substitution is 6(14 - 18 - 1) + 36 = 6. The visible actuator diagram makes the two rigid members of each telescoping leg distinguishable.

The actuator, speed reducer and transmission must be selected together. Direct drive places the actuator at the driven joint and connects its output directly; merely placing a geared motor near the joint is not equivalent. Remote driving moves actuator mass toward the base.

The displayed ideal relations are output speed = input speed / eta and output torque = eta times input torque. Eta denotes reduction ratio, not efficiency. These are ideal magnitude relations despite the separate acknowledgement of friction. The source lists spur, bevel, worm and cross-helical gears. Tighter meshing reduces backlash at a friction cost.

The open-belt drawing labels a smaller input radius r1 and larger output radius r2. Equal belt speed without slip gives eta = r2/r1. Belts and chains carry tension rather than compression, requiring appropriate preload or opposed tension. For unchanged material and section, greater belt length increases compliance. The chain and toothed-belt comparison is a source-specific design comparison.

The lead-screw diagram shows direct threaded nut contact, whereas the ball screw shows rolling balls and a recirculation path. Both convert rotation to translation. The lecture contrasts greater lead-screw friction with lower-friction, typically backdrivable ball screws; no universal self-locking claim follows.

Joint-position sensing plus forward kinematics does not directly measure the loaded end-effector position. Unmodelled deformation and sag can therefore remain. Structural elasticity introduces resonances that constrain useful feedback bandwidth; accurate encoders alone do not remove this limitation.
Parallel k1+k2 and reciprocal series sum explicitly printed. Physical parallel shares displacement, series shares force; transmission springs must be referred to the same shaft before combination.

Actual solid circular shaft k=G*pi*d^4/(32*l), torsional units torque per radian. Output gear k=Cg*b*r² with input gear fixed; face width and output radius specified. Product illustrations do not supply numeric dimensions.

Actual output-referred rotational k_o=eta²*k_i; axial belt AE/l; hollow cantilever transverse round3*pi*E*(do^4−di^4)/(64*l³), squareE*(wo^4−wi^4)/(4*l³). Figure clamped left with downward point force near right tip. Different rotational/axial stiffness units must not be directly added.

Electric actuation interfacing/control advantages and qualified fluid power-to-weight comparison. Brushed DC text says stationary brushes and rotating commutator, current proportional torque, winding heat limit. Generic motor cutaway is not reliable evidence of every brushed component.

Position servo command based on desired versus sensed position error, source recommends sensor on actuator shaft. Co-location does not measure downstream elastic deflection or guarantee global optimality.

Strain gauge bonded to metal, serpentine conductor magnified on cylindrical sensor body. Placement actuator/wrist/fingertips; count, placement, stiffness, sensitivity, overload; wrist commonly3–6 force/torque components, not a claim every gauge arrangement reconstructs6.

Flexure stiffness trades against deflection sensitivity; stops limit overload travel; minimizing welded/bolted joints reduces hysteresis rather than mathematically eliminating all sources. Differential measurements reduce common disturbances; foil durable, semiconductor sensitive but overload-prone.

Mobile robotics integrates mechanics, electronics and computational/cognitive disciplines; moves through facilities rather than fixed reach. Four-wheel blue chassis illustration; kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI and probability named as cooperating fields.

The slide contrasts manipulation of objects with locomotion of the robot through reaction forces against its environment. The fixed-base wording is the introductory contrast, not a restriction on all manipulation. The legged cartoon motivates gait and contact timing; wheeled examples name differential, synchro and omnidirectional drives. The obstacle claim concerns some advanced designs that shift centre of mass, not all wheeled robots.

The source favours wheels for efficiency and mechanical simplicity on flat ground. Its statement that three wheels suffice for stability needs non-collinear contacts and a centre-of-mass projection inside the support polygon under static conditions. The pictured blue chassis has four visible wheels, so it is not a visual proof of a three-wheel assertion. Traction, stability, manoeuvrability and control remain design issues.

Wheel geometry is explicitly both wheel type and wheel arrangement. The text presents tradeoffs among manoeuvrability, controllability and stability, and rejects a universally ideal configuration. Selection depends on task and environment.

The diagram shows a chassis and obstacles inside an enclosing environment. The text gives three planar pose coordinates: x, y and heading theta. The number of pose coordinates is not the number of wheel joints or a guarantee of three independently commandable instantaneous velocities. The workspace statement concerns attainable positions and orientations; the illustration is not a metric map.

The right-hand illustration is a jointed arm with a gripper mounted on a two-wheel side-view chassis. Text describes mobile manipulation, using the base for gross motion and the arm for fine tasks. The lower right outlined rectangle is empty, not a missing labelled mechanism. Adding base motion expands reach but does not eliminate arm limits, obstacles or stability constraints.

The summary integrates actuation, transmission, sensing, stiffness and control. It lists locomotion, perception, localization, cognition and navigation for autonomous mobility. Mobile manipulation combines base and arm motion, with base selection, stability management and configuration-space path planning. The outlined lower-right box is empty and supplies no additional data.

Reference-only page lists Craig, Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control, third edition (2005), and Siegwart and Nourbakhsh, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2004). No new examinable equation or worked example is present.
Closing page contains only Thank You and institutional footer decoration. No substantive concept, numerical premise or figure needs a question.

independentAnswers.reasoning: Seven independent coordinates controlling a regular six-coordinate pose leave one local internal degree of freedom. Redundancy is a coordinate/task-rank comparison, not a requirement for a closed loop.

Intended yes: four independent configuration coordinates minus a rank-three task leave one local degree of freedom. The stem only says four joints, however, so independence and one DOF per joint need to be explicit before this conclusion is guaranteed.

The implicit-function count is local at a reachable regular pose. Joint limits, obstacles and singularities can restrict or destroy a continuous feasible family; extra joints do not make every pose reachable.
A task-preserving internal motion can change the arm posture and therefore its obstacle clearance without moving the tool pose. This is a possible use of redundancy, not a collision-free guarantee.
The source places the extra fast precise small-motion axes at the distal tool, rather than using the whole arm or base for fine correction.
A closed chain contains a kinematic circuit. The visible connection back to the base closes the loop; neither equal link lengths nor a particular joint type is required.
Multiple load paths can improve stiffness, while closure constraints commonly reduce motion range and workspace. Neither zero actuator loads nor unlimited workspace follows.
The source explicitly identifies closed-loop drive structures at Motoman L-3 joints 2 and 3; this is a source-specific example rather than a claim about every robot joint.
The upper member in the figure carries the moving end-effector platform, and the lower horizontal member is the fixed base.
Six variable-length legs act in parallel between the base and moving platform. The source identifies the generic platform as fully parallel with six DOFs.
Each base joint is universal with two rotational freedoms; each platform-end joint is spherical with three. The actuator contributes its separate prismatic freedom.
For a specified platform translation and rotation, both attachment locations are known in a common frame, so each required actuator length is their Euclidean separation.

Under the intended convention, the leg vector is p + R a - b = (0,0,2), whose norm is 2 m. The packet does not define p, a, b or the direction of R, so this answer relies on a conventional interpretation that must be made explicit.
Forward kinematics takes the six given leg lengths and solves for the platform translation and orientation. The reverse direction is the direct attachment-distance calculation.
The printed legend includes ground in the link count. Thus the fixed base contributes to l even though it does not move.
Each of the six legs contributes one universal, one spherical and one prismatic joint. Six times three joint assemblies gives 18.
Each telescoping actuator has two rigid members joined by a prismatic pair. Six actuators therefore contribute twelve links, before adding base and platform.
The freedom sum is 6(2+3+1)=36. Counting freedoms is different from counting the eighteen joints.
Substituting gives 6(14-18-1)+36=-30+36=6. This is the generic mobility prediction, not a nonsingularity certificate.
Mobility counting assumes that the counted constraints are independent. Special geometry can introduce dependencies or special configurations, so rank and geometry must be checked.
The source groups actuator, speed reduction and transmission into an integrated drive design, rather than selecting each in isolation.
Direct drive means that the actuator output attaches directly to the joint; a nearby motor with an intervening reducer is not made direct drive by proximity alone.
Remote actuation places the actuator toward the base, away from the driven joint, with a transmission carrying the motion to that joint.
The four gear types named on the actual slide are spur, bevel, worm and cross-helical. Planetary and harmonic are not in that displayed list.
Reducing clearance by tighter tooth meshing can reduce backlash but increase friction. It does not make friction vanish or change the ratio to zero.
The slide uses eta for the positive input/output speed-magnitude ratio. It is not the efficiency symbol in this context; reciprocal torque and speed conventions must not be confused.
For eta=5, output speed is 100/5=20 rad/s and ideal torque is 5(2)=10 N m. Both sides then transmit 200 W.
The torque multiplication is lossless idealization. Real friction dissipates power, so the ideal torque is not guaranteed for a lossy drive at the same input power and ratio.
Output power is epsilon times input power and output speed is input speed divided by eta. Hence output torque is epsilon eta times input torque: 0.8(5)(2)=8 N m.
A flexible member transmits tension but cannot sustain the commanded push as a rigid compression member. Preload or an opposed tension path is needed for bidirectional force transmission.
Under linear axial elasticity, displacement is Fl/(AE), so compliance l/(AE) grows with length when A and E are fixed.
No slip gives r1 omega1 = r2 omega2. Therefore input/output speed ratio is r2/r1, not its reciprocal or a dimensional sum of radii.
The radius ratio is 60/20=3, so output angular speed is 12/3=4 rad/s.

The lecture describes toothed belts and roller chains as stiffer and more compact, with chains able to wrap smaller pulleys. That qualitative comparison is attributed to the slide, not universalized to all designs.
Rotation of a screw relative to its nut generates relative axial translation. Both illustrated mechanisms implement rotary-to-linear conversion.
The lead screw carries load through direct thread contact. The ball-screw cutaway shows intervening rolling balls and their return path.
The lecture associates ball recirculation with reduced friction and typical backdrivability. Rolling contact does not guarantee self-locking.
An axial external load can drive a backdrivable screw and hence its input shaft. A suspended load therefore needs an appropriate holding measure rather than assuming the screw locks itself.
Rigid forward kinematics does not include unmeasured elastic link or transmission deformation. Accurate joint sensing can coexist with a loaded tool-position error.
Compliance creates mechanical resonances, which can constrain useful control bandwidth. It does not imply infinite stiffness or removal of vibration.
Parallel springs experience a common displacement; summing their forces gives F=(k1+k2) delta, hence their stiffnesses add.
Series springs share force and their displacements add. Thus k=1/(1/100+1/300)=75 N/m.
Parallel stiffness is 100+300=400 N/m. A total force of 40 N gives common displacement 40/400=0.1 m.
For positive finite k1 and k2, 1/k_eq=1/k1+1/k2 exceeds either reciprocal; k_eq is therefore smaller than either stiffness.
Refer the input spring through the reducer first: 3 squared times 100=900 N m/rad. Two output-referred 900 springs in series give 450 N m/rad.
The circular solid-shaft torsion formula contains d to the fourth power. Length enters inversely and shear modulus linearly.
Doubling d multiplies d to the fourth power by 16, while unchanged G and l leave every other factor unchanged.
Torsional stiffness is inversely proportional to length, so doubling length halves stiffness. With torque fixed, twist equals torque/stiffness and doubles.
G pi d^4/(32 l) = (80 times 10^9) pi (0.02)^4/(32 times 0.5) = 800 pi = 2513.274... N m/rad. This is rotational, not axial, stiffness.
The scale factor is 2 times (1/2)^2 = 1/2. Doubling face width cannot offset a squared reduction in radius.
The slide specifies a fixed input gear while estimating output-gear stiffness; the measured elastic displacement is on the output side.
Ideal reduction multiplies torque by eta and divides the corresponding input elastic angle by eta. Their ratio therefore gains eta squared.
Convert 2 mm squared to 2 times 10^-6 m squared and 1 GPa to 10^9 N/m squared. AE/l=(2 times 10^-6)(10^9)/0.5=4000 N/m.
Torque per angular displacement has units N m/rad; axial force per extension has units N/m. They must be referred to compatible coordinates before combination.
As the inner diameter approaches the fixed outer diameter, d_o^4-d_i^4 tends to zero, so the ideal bending stiffness tends to zero.
Both cantilever formulas contain length cubed in the denominator. Doubling length multiplies the denominator by eight and stiffness by one eighth.
Relative to the solid section with the same outer diameter, the retained fraction is 1-(d_i/d_o)^4=1-(1/2)^4=15/16.
The square-section second moment is proportional to outer width to the fourth power minus inner width to the fourth power, not their sum or squared difference.
The pictured beam is clamped at one end and loaded transversely at the free end. The stated stiffness is the small-deflection end-point force/displacement relation for that cantilever condition.
Electrical interfacing and precise control are the stated advantages. The source does not assert universal superiority in power-to-weight or absence of thermal limits.
Stationary brushes contact the rotating commutator, supplying current to the rotor windings. Reversing those rotating/stationary roles does not match the described motor.
The slide identifies winding overheating as a primary operating limitation. Other real limitations are not the specifically named answer here.
In the stated linear constant-flux model, torque is K_t I = 0.4 times 3 = 1.2 N m.
The servo error used here is desired minus measured position. The controller converts that position discrepancy into an actuator force or torque command.
The prescribed error convention gives 30 degrees minus 26 degrees = positive 4 degrees. It is an angle, not an angular speed.
Co-location in this slide means the position sensor is on the actuator shaft, measuring the same local actuator coordinate.
A shaft encoder measures the actuator-side coordinate, not every downstream deformation. Flexible transmission can therefore produce loaded tool error despite exact shaft measurement.
The bonded gauge responds to local material strain; force or moment requires a calibrated mechanical and electrical relation from that strain.
The slide lists joint actuators, wrist joints and end-effector fingertips as force-sensing locations.
A full spatial wrench consists of three directed force components and three moment components. This applies to the stipulated six-axis device, not automatically every three-component sensor.
The inset visibly shows a serpentine strain-gauge conductor and its leads bonded to the mechanical flexure, not an encoder or screw mechanism.
Gauge number and placement affect measurable components, while stiffness, sensitivity and overload protection are concurrent design considerations.
A scalar linear flexure obeys F=k delta, hence displacement sensitivity delta/F is 1/k. Increasing k reduces that sensitivity with readout gain held fixed.
Mechanical stops cap excessive flexure displacement before damaging deformation. They neither remove calibration requirements nor create infinite sensitivity.
Removing interfaces can reduce an interface-related contribution to hysteresis. Material, electronics or other causes can remain; zero hysteresis is not guaranteed.
Subtracting gives (s+b)-(-s+b)=2s; dividing by two returns s. The identical common-mode bias cancels.
The slide describes metal foil as more durable but less sensitive, and semiconductor gauges as more sensitive but more vulnerable to overload.
A mobile robot can relocate its own base through the environment rather than being tied to a fixed installation. This alone does not guarantee larger arm reach or require wheels instead of legs.
The lecture explicitly combines kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI and probability. Its interdisciplinary framing excludes a mechanics-only or computation-only approach.
In the slide's illustrative contrast, manipulation changes object motion while locomotion changes the robot's position relative to its environment through contact forces.
Gait coordinates the ordering and timing of lift and contact events among legs, rather than merely counting joints or specifying average speed.
Differential, synchro and omnidirectional are the three drive families explicitly named on the source page.
The statement concerns advanced wheeled designs that actively shift centre of mass to negotiate obstacles larger than wheel diameter; it is not a guarantee for every terrain or drive layout.
The source links rolling efficiency and mechanical simplicity to flat-ground operation. The claim is conditional on that operating context, not every terrain.

For static gravity loading, support contacts must span a nonzero area and the combined COM projection must lie within their support triangle. Three equal wheel diameters or motor currents do not establish that condition.
Under the explicitly stated support criterion, a COM projection outside the support polygon removes static equilibrium stability even with unchanged wheel count.
Wheel geometry includes both the type of wheel and its spatial arrangement. Diameter or motor settings alone omit important parts of the definition.
The absence of a universally ideal layout calls for matching terrain, stability, manoeuvrability and control requirements to the application, rather than optimizing a single count or metric.
A planar rigid pose needs two translation coordinates and one heading: (x,y,theta). Wheel angles or force components are not a replacement for pose.
Wheel and actuator counts can increase internal state dimension, but the planar rigid chassis still has three pose coordinates.

A no-side-slip velocity constraint restricts instantaneous motion, not the validity of the three-coordinate configuration description. A sequence of turning and forward motions can still change lateral position.
The lecture defines workspace through attainable positions and orientations within the environment, not all drawn points or motor commands.
The actual illustration shows an articulated arm ending in a gripper on a wheeled chassis. It is neither a bare chassis nor a fixed pedestal arm.
The stated division is gross relocation by the mobile base and fine local tasks by the arm. This is a useful division of roles, not a statement that either subsystem never moves otherwise.
Mobile-base motion expands the reachable set but does not remove obstacles, arm joint limits, base access constraints or stability requirements.
The five named competence areas are locomotion, perception, localization, cognition and navigation.
An arm extends beyond the base centre and changes the combined geometry and mass distribution. Base-centre collision freedom alone therefore cannot certify whole-robot clearance or stability.
The summary explicitly calls for co-design of actuation, transmission, sensing, stiffness and control. Ignoring compliance or postponing stability indefinitely contradicts that integrated approach.

The lecture's qualitative comparison assigns electric actuation lower power-to-weight than fluid actuation while emphasizing suitability for precision control. This is recorded as a source claim, not a current market survey.

blindnessDisclosure: All answers were derived from the answer-free packet and actual supplied source pixels before opening author keys, solutions, generators, checks or findings. Source slides can themselves contain worked answers; blind means not exposed to the proposed question key or author solution.
